claims.text: Actively learned moment-tensor potentials can be parameterized using ab initio data in finite-temperature multicomponent-alloy workflows.
An MTP trained on configurations sampled at and around fusion can accurately reproduce the ab initio energy landscape relevant to melting.
The proposed MTP can accurately reproduce solid-phase free energies near melting.
The proposed MTP can accurately reproduce liquid-phase free energies near melting.
The proposed workflow retains vibrational-entropy contributions to fusion free energies.
The proposed workflow retains anharmonic contributions to fusion free energies.
The proposed MTP captures electron-vibration coupling effects pertinent to melting.
Active learning ensures that configurations critical for vibrational and anharmonic effects are included in the training set.
Using the MTP in thermodynamic integration permits calculation of solid and liquid free energies without full explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The MTP-based workflow will substantially reduce computational cost relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy calculations.
The MTP-based workflow will substantially reduce computational cost relative to TOR-TILD.
The workflow may be at least an order of magnitude faster than explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
For elemental or binary systems, predicted fusion free energies will deviate by no more than approximately 10% from established ab initio or TOR-TILD results.
The active-learning MTP approach can scale from elemental and binary systems to multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The method should work reliably near melting when thermal disorder is dominant.
Accuracy may deteriorate at very low temperatures or in systems with strong quantum effects.
Accuracy depends on how representative the ab initio active-learning data are.
The cited evidence supplies prior elemental or binary fusion-free-energy results supporting the proposed method.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and mediator state categorically that the MTP captures electron-vibration effects, whereas the uncertainty field says that capturing electron-vibration coupling solely through the potential is uncertain.
